synopsis: DynoTRAIN built the simulation-validation method behind the European rail running-approval standard EN 14363, with project results published in 2014–2015 and a broader EN 14363/DynoTRAIN acceptance-extension case spanning 2014–2022 [f14671, f14677, f7854]. Its research compared several vehicle models and software tools with measurements from multiple vehicles and countries, using more than 1,000 simulations [f7711, f14678]. Because engineering judgment applied to large numbers of plots did not scale, DynoTRAIN developed objective validation metrics; the resulting practice uses at least 24 simulation-versus-measurement comparisons per quantity from at least 12 track sections, with limits on comparison-set means and standard deviations [f7712, f14680]. The EN 14363 framework with ERA guidance addresses extended test conditions, modified vehicles and approved-reference-vehicle comparisons, while retaining physical running tests for the reference vehicle [f8135, f8136]. The corpus identifies this as the strongest family-transfer and test-reduction precedent for off-road automatic braking, but reports neither formal risk scaling nor a published percentage of physical tests removed across actual rail certifications [f8137, f8132, f7856].
